articles.title: Compress Any Image to Exactly 100KB: A Binary-Search Trick
articles.excerpt: Every web developer has lived this exact loop: A form says "upload must be under 100KB". You export your image at quality 80. It's 340KB. You drop to 60. It's 61KB — nice. Or it's 134KB — not nice. Yo…
articles.body: Every web developer has lived this exact loop: A form says "upload must be under 100KB". You export your image at quality 80. It's 340KB. You drop to 60. It's 61KB — nice. Or it's 134KB — not nice. You try 55. It's 98KB. Close enough. Ship it. Ten minutes of blind guessing to satisfy one number. And the number you were actually asked about — the file size — was never under your control. You were tuning a proxy (the quality slider) and hoping the size landed somewhere acceptable. There's a better primitive, and it works every single time. Why the quality slider is the wrong primitive Here's the uncomfortable truth about the quality slider: the same quality value produces wildly different file sizes on different images. A flat illustration at quality 80 might be 40KB.

articles.body: Rapid user actions can crash Android WebViews when file selection prompts overlap. Quick solution: filePathCallback ?. onReceiveValue ( null ) filePathCallback = newCallback Prerequisites require setting up an ActivityResultLauncher registered via the Android Activity Result APIs before launching intents. Developers must ensure that any active callback is explicitly resolved before accepting a new one, as detailed in the official Android WebChromeClient reference . What happens when a second chooser replaces the first? Each invocation of onShowFileChooser delivers a fresh ValueCallback reference. If a user taps an upload button, switches away, and taps another upload button without resolving the first, the framework expects the host app to finish the pending request.

articles.title: Map WebDAV to a Real Drive Letter on Windows: Network Location vs. Volume
articles.excerpt: Every "mount my NAS in Explorer" guide starts with Map Network Drive, and most of them stop right there. The trap is that what Windows gives you in that dialog is not actually a drive. Three things yo…
articles.body: Every "mount my NAS in Explorer" guide starts with Map Network Drive , and most of them stop right there. The trap is that what Windows gives you in that dialog is not actually a drive. Three things you only discover after hitting the wall: Network location, not volume. The share shows up in the Explorer tree, but anything that enumerates volumes — backup agents, imaging tools, older installers, some indexers — never sees it. If you have ever watched a backup tool cheerfully report "no such drive" for files you can plainly see, this is why. No LOCK/UNLOCK. The built-in WebDAV client does not implement WebDAV locking, so applications that lock files (Office among them) treat the file as read-only or fail outright.

articles.title: My HTML-to-Markdown API learned that every framework invents its own idea of a heading
articles.excerpt: I built the HTML-to-Markdown converter expecting a boring job: walk the DOM, emit # for , ## for , done. The first real-world test was a Next.js docs site, and it came back as a wall of bold text with…
articles.body: I built the HTML-to-Markdown converter expecting a boring job: walk the DOM, emit # for <h1> , ## for <h2> , done. The first real-world test was a Next.js docs site, and it came back as a wall of bold text with zero heading structure. The culprit: Tailwind. The site styled <div class="text-2xl font-bold mb-4"> as its visual headings. No <h1> tags anywhere. Semantically it was a disaster, visually it was a perfectly good docs page. My converter saw divs and shrugged. The fix wasn't smarter HTML parsing — it was admitting that "heading" is a visual concept, not a tag concept.

articles.excerpt: Cooking Up Magick Book Review
articles.body: The first book in a new series called The Dell Chronicles, HL Bernabe’s Cooking Up Magick sets out to be a cozier fantasy version of The Lord of the Rings . And in many ways, it does pull directly from J.R.R. Tolkien’s world. The main character, Paisley, is a halfling who gets swept up on an adventure with a pair of dwarves, but unbeknownst to her, there’s also an evil overlord that has just returned after centuries – and she’s the only hope the world has to actually stop him. The similarities to The Hobbit and LOTR pretty much end there though, and you don’t get nearly enough detail in the first book to effectively flesh out this alternate version of Middle-earth. What you do get is a lovable main character who is surrounded by an interesting cast of characters.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 20, 1970: The Soviet Union launches last-ever Zond moon mission
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 20, 1970, the Soviet Union launched the Zond 8 spacecraft on a mission to the moon. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 20, 1970, the Soviet Union launched the Zond 8 spacecraft on a mission to the moon. This was the last mission in the Zond program. After the first three Zond missions explored Venus and Mars , the next ones were circumlunar missions that flew around the moon before returning to Earth. Although there was no crew on board, the Zond spacecraft was designed with cosmonauts in mind. The Zond missions served as test flights for the Soviet Union's plans to send cosmonauts to the moon. But those plans for crewed flights never came to fruition. This was partly because the U.S. had already put astronauts on the moon , but also because the Zond missions had a lot of technical problems. Zond 8 was considered a success — even though its guidance system malfunctioned on the way back to Earth.
